Editorial & Evidence Policy

This page explains how Ruang Tanpa Stigma selects sources, checks claims, reviews language, reports review status and corrects health content.

Policy ownerRuang Tanpa Stigma

Last updated19 September 2026

Policy cycleAnnually or earlier when needed

On this page

  1. 01Source hierarchy
  2. 02Editorial workflow
  3. 03Status & metadata
  4. 04Review schedule
  5. 05Corrections
  6. 06Respectful language

01 · Source hierarchy

Indonesian context comes first.

Indonesia-specific information

Indonesia’s Ministry of Health, official Indonesian health authorities, and national clinical or public-health guidance are the primary references for policy, service pathways and local context.

International sources

WHO and UNAIDS are prioritized for HIV basics, prevention, treatment, U=U, stigma, rights and international recommendations. Other authoritative health bodies are used when relevant and their scope is clear.

Scientific literature

Peer-reviewed literature is used when guidance needs added context or content discusses behaviour, stigma, treatment engagement, health communication or community research.

Random blogs, unsourced content, social-media posts and promotional materials are not used as the sole basis for medical claims.

02 · Editorial workflow

Each claim passes through several checks.

Draft → source verification → claim check → language review → clinical/public-health review when required → publication → scheduled review

  • Draft: define the purpose, audience and scope.
  • Source verification: open and check primary or authoritative sources directly.
  • Claim check: keep wording within the evidence, including U=U’s scope for sexual transmission.
  • Language review: explain terms, shorten dense passages and remove stigmatizing language.
  • Professional review: obtain it when clinical or safety content requires it and display it only after it has genuinely occurred.
  • Publication and review: record dates, sources and review status in public or editorial metadata.

03 · Status & metadata

Honest status matters more than an appearance of perfection.

Content may use the internal statuses Draft, Source checked, Needs clinical review, Independently reviewed and Published. Not every status needs a prominent public badge, but it must remain traceable in the editorial system.

Major medical pages support an author or responsible owner, publication date where relevant, last review date, review cycle or next review, authoritative sources, clinical-review need and review status.

If no qualified external reviewer has completed a review, the page will state not yet independently clinically reviewed. Reviewer names, credentials and affiliations are never invented.

04 · Review schedule

A review date should mean something.

The baseline target for substantial medical education pages is review at least annually. Earlier review is triggered when Ministry of Health, WHO or UNAIDS guidance changes; an important source link fails; or a safety risk, ambiguity or error is identified.

A new review date is added only after the content and its sources have actually been checked. Changing a date without performing the review is not allowed.

05 · Corrections policy

Health guidance changes, and errors should be corrected openly.

  • Factual errors, broken sources and potentially harmful wording are addressed as soon as reasonably possible.
  • Substantial corrections record a date and summary in the editorial changelog.
  • Content is updated when authoritative guidance changes.
  • If a page cannot be updated safely at once, its status or publication may be withheld.

V2 starts a changelog for meaningful editorial changes. It does not invent a corrections history from before this process existed.

06 · Language policy

Language shapes how people are treated.

We use person-centred language and do not reduce someone to a diagnosis. In suitable contexts, we use phrases such as people living with HIV. Terms implying victimhood, contamination or danger are avoided unless explaining why that language causes harm.

We also do not rigidly police how people identify themselves. Respect for identity, context and lived experience still matters.

Bahasa Indonesia is written and reviewed as the primary language, not as a literal translation. English is written to sound natural while preserving the same medical scope.
